nameStory: The Garden Snail earned its common name simply because it's the snail you're most likely to encounter in gardens, where it munches on plants to the frustration of many gardeners. This humble mollusk has become so associated with backyard gardening that 'garden snail' is recognized worldwide, even though it originally hails from the Mediterranean region.
description: The Garden Snail is a medium-sized land snail with a round, spiral shell that's typically brown with darker bands or mottled patterns. Adults usually reach about 1-1.5 inches across, making them one of the larger snails you'll see crawling around New England yards. When active, they extend a grayish body with four tentacles - two longer ones with eyes at the tips, and two shorter ones used for smell and touch. Their shells can vary from light tan to dark brown, often with subtle stripes or speckled patterns.

idTips.label: Shell size and shape
idTips.description: Round, globe-like shell about the size of a large marble, with 4-5 whorls spiraling clockwise when viewed from above. The shell feels smooth but solid, like polished ceramic.

idTips.label: Shell coloration
idTips.description: Brown shell with darker brown bands or mottled patterns, sometimes appearing almost striped. The colors can range from light tan to deep chocolate brown.

idTips.label: Body appearance
idTips.description: Grayish, slimy body that can extend to nearly twice the shell's length. Touch the extended body gently and it will quickly retract with surprising speed.

idTips.label: Tentacles
idTips.description: Four tentacles when fully extended - two long ones with dark eye spots at the tips, and two shorter ones below. They feel soft and wet, and will instantly pull back if touched.

idTips.label: Slime trail
idTips.description: Leaves a distinctive shiny, sticky trail that feels slippery between your fingers and can be seen glistening on surfaces even after the snail has passed.

habitat: Garden Snails thrive in moist, sheltered areas around human habitation, particularly vegetable and flower gardens where they find abundant food. Look for them under plant pots, garden stones, mulch, or in compost piles where the soil stays damp. They prefer areas with some calcium in the soil (which they need for shell building) and are most common in suburban and urban settings rather than deep wilderness.

seasonality.spring: Snails become active again as temperatures warm and moisture increases from spring rains. Look for them emerging from winter hiding spots under stones or buried in leaf litter.
seasonality.summer: Most active during humid summer evenings and after rain showers, when you'll spot them crawling across sidewalks and garden paths. During hot, dry spells they'll retreat and seal their shell openings.
seasonality.fall: Continue feeding actively to prepare for winter, often seen on cool, dewy mornings. They may start seeking out protected overwintering sites under mulch or stones.
seasonality.winter: Largely inactive, sealed inside their shells in protected spots like under rocks, logs, or deep in mulch piles. Their shell opening is covered with a temporary 'door' of dried mucus.

funFact: Garden Snails are both male and female at the same time (hermaphrodites), but they still need to mate with another snail - and during courtship, they literally shoot calcium 'love darts' into each other to increase the chances of successful reproduction!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with native woodland snails, but Garden Snails are noticeably larger and rounder, and you'll rarely find them far from human development. Remember: 'Garden snails stick close to gardens' - if you find a similar snail deep in the woods, it's probably a native species.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'Garden Snail,' this species is actually non-native to New England, originally from the Mediterranean region. It's the same species eaten as escargot in French cuisine, and while considered a pest by most New England gardeners, it's actually prized as food in many parts of the world.
compareHints: Since Garden Snails are the only Cornu species in New England, compare them to other common land snails in the Helicidae family. Garden Snails are significantly larger and more robust than most native woodland snails, with thicker, more globular shells. Unlike the flatter, more disc-like shells of some native species, Garden Snails have distinctly rounded, 'bubble-like' shells that are noticeably heavier when picked up.
